cotton growers of the Georgia and South Caro-
lina coast, the sugar planters of Louisiana,
and the great cotton planters of the bottom
lands of the Mississippi, Red, Ouachita,
Arkansas, Alabama, Black Warrior, and other
rivers.

It was these men, or their representatives
in politics, who caused secession, and they
did it because they wanted to establish a
slaveholding oligarchy. They were nearly
all democrats. Through the potency of the
democratic name they induced the non-slave-
holders and the small upland farmers to unite
with them.

aids of Douglas, and Toombs was in the
United States senate as a democrat when secession came. Judah P. Benjamin renounced
his allegiance to the whig party at the same
time Toombs and Stephens did. Ben Hill
never had any politics that lasted long. He
was whig, know nothing, or democrat, union
man or secessionist, as it suited his conven-
ience.

who will bow down before their false gods.
Garland and Walker, the senators from Ar-
kansas, were both whigs before the war, and
Walker beat the acknowledged leader of the
old democracy "Bob" Johnson—for his seat

ened, confident that her mother was not
there, being personally acquainted with
nearly all the inmates.

was removed by friends to Kutztown. The
daughter, now a woman thirty-six years of
age, has expressed wish to lead a differ-
ent life than subsisting on public charity,
and will be taken away in a few days.

To the Editor Of the Dispatch:


Will the Dispatch tell us exactly what
the provision of the force bill" which
Randall defeated was! My recollection is
that one of its provisions was to place the

States entirely in the hands of deputy mar-

ral Constitution forbids the suspension of

vasion, it was necessary also for the Radi-

bellion"; and this the force bill did by

declare that there was rebellion, and then

cause there was rebellion. Treason to
liberty and to the United States Govern-
ment, and to the people, was the crime of
the men who conceived this bill and en-

Fresh mullet from Ocklockonee Bay are selling for a dollar.

The brick for the agricultural college at Lake City can be burned within a half mile of the site.

Money is being subscribed to build a church at Fort Mason. It will be thrown open to all denominations.

It is rumored that the Sanford House, at Sanford, will be kept open the whole year round hereafter.

A petition has been sent to Washington requesting that a Signal station be established at Apalachicola.

Quincy's Artesian Well Committee are doing all they can to find out what it will cost to have well bored.

Pensacola has a new machine shop in which is being built one of the smallest locomotives in the United States.

Fifteen of the 3,091 officers and employees of the United States Treasury Department were appointed from Florida.

There is at the Waycross depot a complete sawmill, including engine and boiler, for Constantine X DeBois, of Waitsfield, Fla.

It is rumored that Orange City will have by the 1st of January a bank with a capital of $300,000, to be opened by an Ohio gentleman.

Mr. King, of Manatee, who has been practicing attorney, intends applying for admission to the bar of the circuit at the fall term of court.

The banana tree of J. W. Funk, of Lake City, sent to Louisville, is said to be in excellent condition, and is one of the best specimens on the ground.

There are seven saw mills in Suwannee county, and others going up. Some of these mills have capacity of from 10,000 to 10,000 feet of lumber per day.

Mayor Dancy, of Jacksonville, has notified the Express Company that messengers or packages from Pensacola will not be allowed to come or be brought inside the city limits.

J. J. Flemming has been appointed Weigher and Gauger at the custom house at Key West. Hon. J. W. Menard has been appointed Principal of Douglass school, at the same place.

The liquor case of Charles Q. Elliott vs. J. J. Brown, Collector of Revenue, which was argued before Judge Baker at chambers a few days ago, has been decided in favor of the local option law.

The Clay Guards, of Green Cove Springs, will have dress parade this afternoon, and have sent out invitations to a complimentary ball to take place later in the evening. The Guards are but three-months-old organization.

The orange crop of Orange county is considered the largest and finest ever gathered, but very few are splitting, notwithstanding the frequent heavy rains have given an unusually heavy flow of sap, which is the cause of the splitting.

The steamer Bertha Lee has arrived at Fort Myers in the interest of the Kissimmee, Okeechobee and Gulf Navigation Company, to make weekly trips from Punta Rassa to Kissimmee city, with freight and passengers through the canal.

The imports into Jacksonville port, brought by sailing vessels for the month of September, outside of general merchandise, fertilizers, lime, hay, etc., were 1,921 tons and $50 steel rails, 10 tons of ice and $50 tons of broken stone for the jetties.

A meeting is called to take place at Fort Mason on Saturday, October 18th, for the purpose of forming a fruit and vegetable association, to bring about concert of action in shipments and to protect the planters and shippers in their manifold interests.

The report that a case of yellow fever has developed in Pensacola had its origin in the death of a dissolute woman whose ailment is claimed by the Commercial to have been another disease. The Coroner and the Board of Health are at swords points.

The vestry and congregation of St. Paul's Church, in Key West, have, during the rector's absence, put a new roof on the rectory building, and since his return have raised funds for the purpose of adding a piazza to the lower and upper stories in the front of it.

Mr. Joseph Cobb, a cripple, who came to Jacksonville several years ago for the benefit of his health, having been a sufferer from rheumatism for a number of years, died on Sunday morning and was buried Monday afternoon by the jewellers from Mr. B. T. Oaks' establishment.

About a mile from Tavares on an old deserted 'deadening' may be seen a century plant which will soon be in bloom. A spear has been shot up to the height of about twenty-five feet, and eight branches have grown out, from which smaller branches or buds are growing.

Last Saturday night Elbert Hemming, his wife, and their cousin, Miss Mamie Dupont, with their cook, residing at Jacksonville, were poisoned by eating shrimps which had been boiled in a boiler which had a copper bottom. Monday all had recovered from the effects but Mr. Hemming.

Mr. Richardson, of Duval county, raised a vestige of white yam, which measured twenty-four and a half inches in circumference and weighed seven and a half pounds. The yam was grown on Mr. Richardson's farm, about fifteen miles from Jacksonville, and will be forwarded to the Louisville exposition.

The young misses are not yet in their teens, and deserve all praise, both for their industry and true charity.
